title: The Journey of Jules Barbier — Paris and the Myths Made Song
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Boulevards — a Paris poet is born (1825-1852)

stops.name: Paris — birth, 7 Rue Marie-Éléonore-de-Bellefond
stops.campa: In a modest house on the Rue Marie-Éléonore-de-Bellefond, north of the grands boulevards, a son is born to the family Barbier and is named Paul Jules. The Restoration is at its height; the July Revolution is still five years off. He will scarcely leave this city his whole life long — and yet through his pen half the myths of Europe will pass into song. The boy who cannot travel will send Faust, Mignon, Sheba, and Joan travelling for him, across the lyric stage of a whole century.
suggested_refs: Map of the 9th arrondissement, Second Empire

stops.name: Comédie-Française — the debut, L'Ombre de Molière
stops.campa: The young poet makes his entrance on the first stage of France. His intermède L'Ombre de Molière — the Shade of Molière — is given at the Comédie-Française in 1847, a boy of twenty-one summoning the ghost of the great comic master to bless his own beginnings. It is a poet's homage and a poet's calling card: verse for the theatre, the form that will hold him for fifty years. He is a man of the boulevards now, at home among the vaudevillistes and the lyric hacks, learning the trade that turns literature into an evening's spectacle.
suggested_refs: Bust of Molière, foyer of the Comédie-Française

stops.name: The vaudevilles and the young verse — the boulevards of the 1840s
stops.campa: Through the smoky little houses of the boulevard du Temple — the Boulevard du Crime, thick with melodrama and one-act farce — the apprentice librettist earns his living. He writes comedies, vaudevilles, and verse, collaborating with the reigning craftsmen of the light stage, Labiche among them. Amour et Bergerie is given at the Théâtre-Français in 1848. It is a schooling in what an audience will bear: how a line must scan to be sung, how a scene must turn to hold a house. The gravity of Goethe is still years away; first, the poet learns to please.
suggested_refs: Engraving of the Boulevard du Temple ('Boulevard du Crime')

segments.name: The Pen of Two Heads — Carré et Barbier (1849-1853)

stops.name: The partnership with Michel Carré begins — a two-headed pen
stops.campa: About the year 1849 Barbier joins his name to another, and the joined name — Carré et Barbier — becomes one of the great signatures of the French lyric stage. Michel Carré is his elder, his match, his second self; for more than twenty years the two write as a single pen, so seamlessly that no one can say which line is whose. Together they will clothe Goethe, Shakespeare, Ovid, Corneille, Dante, and the Bible in French verse fit for music. The Second Empire's opera is about to find its poets.
suggested_refs: Joint signature 'Barbier et Carré' on a libretto title page

stops.name: Opéra-Comique (Salle Favart) — Les Noces de Jeannette, the first success
stops.campa: On 4 February 1853 the Salle Favart gives Les Noces de Jeannette, a one-act opéra-comique to Victor Massé's music and the words of Carré and Barbier. Caroline Miolan-Carvalho is the peasant bride Jeannette who tames her runaway groom over a night of song. It is a slight thing and an immortal one: the little wedding will run for a thousand nights and more, past the century's end. For the two young librettists it is the first great hit, the proof that their pen can fill a house. The partnership is launched; the great libretti are coming.
suggested_refs: Score cover of Les Noces de Jeannette (Massé)
Portrait of Caroline Miolan-Carvalho as Jeannette

segments.name: The Myths Made Song — Goethe, Ovid, Solomon (1858-1866)

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique (boulevard du Temple) — LE MÉDECIN MALGRÉ LUI: Molière set
stops.campa: On 15 January 1858 the Théâtre-Lyrique gives Gounod's Le Médecin malgré lui, Barbier and Carré after Molière — the shade the young Barbier had once summoned now fully served. Sganarelle the drunken faggot-gatherer, beaten into playing a doctor, cures by nonsense and gets rich by fraud: Molière's farce set nimbly to music, with mock-Latin and a wagging tongue. Berlioz praises its wit in the Journal des débats. It is the pair's first Gounod collaboration to reach the stage, the dress rehearsal for a partnership that will next give the world its Faust — comedy before the tragedy, the craft warming up.
suggested_refs: Score cover of Le Médecin malgré lui (Gounod)
Molière, Le Médecin malgré lui, frontispiece

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique (boulevard du Temple) — FAUST: Goethe made song
stops.campa: On 19 March 1859 the Théâtre-Lyrique, then on the boulevard du Temple, gives Gounod's Faust to the words of Barbier and Carré — and the corpus's own Goethe becomes opera. Marguerite sits at the spinning-wheel; she opens the casket and the Jewel Song spills out, 'Ah! je ris de me voir si belle en ce miroir!' The demon answers her prayer at the church door; and at the last, from the scaffold, the voices climb — 'Sauvée!' — and she ascends. Faust's despairing bargain, the seduction, the ruin, the redemption: the German tragedy Goethe forged is now sung in French, night after night, the most famous of all French operas.
stops.quote: Ah ! je ris de me voir si belle en ce miroir ! Est-ce toi, Marguerite ? Réponds-moi, réponds vite !
stops.quote_source: Faust (Gounod), Act III, the Jewel Song / Air des bijoux — libretto Barbier & Carré
suggested_refs: Manuscript score of the Jewel Song

stops.name: Goethe's own journey — the Faust legend faced across the atlas
stops.campa: The opera turns, and the myth it enters is Goethe's own. This stop faces the Goethe journey directly: the poet of Weimar who took the old German tale of the scholar who sold his soul and made of it the epic of the modern spirit. Barbier's Marguerite is Goethe's Gretchen; the church scene, the prison, the final ascension are Goethe's own architecture, carried whole into song. Where Goethe wrote for the study and the German stage, Barbier writes for the Parisian pit — the same Faust, doubled: once in verse to be read, once in verse to be sung.
stops.quote: Kennst du das Land, wo die Zitronen blühn?
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre — the source-world Barbier will himself set as Mignon

stops.name: Opéra-Comique (Salle Favart) — LE PARDON DE PLOËRMEL: the Breton shadow-dance
stops.campa: On 4 April 1859, sixteen days after Faust, the Salle Favart gives Meyerbeer's Le Pardon de Ploërmel — later Dinorah — Barbier and Carré after two Breton tales of Souvestre. The goatherd Dinorah, driven half-mad by a lost bridegroom and a treasure-hunt, wanders the moor and, catching her own shadow in the moonlight, sings and waltzes with it: 'Ombre légère,' the Shadow Song, a coloratura chasing its own echo. It is Barbier's one great libretto for Meyerbeer, the aging master of grand opéra, and a strange sister to the singing doll he will write two decades hence — the self mistaken for another.
stops.quote: Ombre légère qui suis mes pas, ne t'en va pas ! Non, non, non !
stops.quote_source: Le Pardon de Ploërmel (Meyerbeer), the Shadow Song — libretto Barbier & Carré
suggested_refs: Poster for Dinorah / Le Pardon de Ploërmel

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique (boulevard du Temple) — PHILÉMON ET BAUCIS: Ovid at the door
stops.campa: On 18 February 1860 the same Théâtre-Lyrique gives Gounod's Philémon et Baucis, Ovid by way of La Fontaine, in three acts by Barbier and Carré. Jupiter and Vulcan, disguised as weary travellers, are turned from every proud door until an old poor couple — Philémon and Baucis — take them in and share their little all. The gods reward the two with restored youth and a shared death, changed at the end into intertwined trees. It is the Metamorphoses on the lyric stage: hospitality rewarded, love made deathless, the antique world sung in the accent of the Second Empire.
suggested_refs: Score cover of Philémon et Baucis (Gounod)
Rubens, Jupiter and Mercury in the House of Philemon and Baucis

stops.name: Ovid's Phrygia — the myth of the pious couple
stops.campa: The myth the opera enters lies in the hills of Phrygia, where Ovid set the tale. Two gods walk the earth as beggars; a whole village bars its doors; only in the humblest cottage, under a thatched roof, are they welcomed with what little there is — and the little is enough. The lake that drowns the inhospitable town spares the faithful hut, which becomes a temple; and the old couple, asked their wish, ask only to die together and never see the other's grave. Barbier gives this most tender of the Metamorphoses a French mouth and a Gounod melody.
suggested_refs: Adam Elsheimer, Jupiter and Mercury in the House of Philemon and Baucis

stops.name: Opéra (Salle Le Peletier) — LA REINE DE SABA: Sheba, Solomon, and the Temple builder
stops.campa: On 28 February 1862 the Paris Opéra at the Salle Le Peletier gives Gounod's grand opera La Reine de Saba, words by Barbier and Carré after Nerval. Balkis, Queen of Sheba, comes to the court of Soliman — but loves not the king; she loves Adoniram, the artisan who casts the sea of bronze for the Temple. It is the Hiram legend, the master-builder of Solomon's Temple murdered by his three treacherous workmen: the very heart of the Masonic myth, so plainly that some whispered Napoleon III himself had the work suppressed after fifteen nights. Sheba and Solomon, the Temple and its builder — all made song.
stops.quote: Inspirez-moi, race divine, enfants de Tubal-Caïn !
stops.quote_source: La Reine de Saba (Gounod), Adoniram's air — libretto Barbier & Carré
suggested_refs: Score cover of La Reine de Saba (Gounod)

stops.name: The court of Solomon — Sheba and the Temple faced across the atlas
stops.campa: The myth the opera enters is Jerusalem in the age of the Temple — this stop faces our Sheba and Solomon journeys at once. The Queen of the South comes with camels bearing spices and gold to prove the wise king with hard questions; and behind them both stands the builder, Hiram-Adoniram, whose bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz frame the sanctuary door. Where scripture makes Sheba a marvel of homage and Hiram a craftsman of the first Temple, Barbier's libretto binds the three in a single tragic knot — queen, king, and artisan — and hands the Masonic Temple-legend to the operatic stage.
stops.quote: And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom... there was no more spirit in her.
stops.quote_source: 1 Kings 10 — the scriptural source-world the libretto dramatizes
suggested_refs: Piero della Francesca, Meeting of Solomon and Sheba
Solomon's Temple reconstruction with Jachin and Boaz
sources: Cross-reference: sheba.journey.json and solomon.journey.json in the atlas

stops.name: Opéra-Comique (Salle Favart) — MIGNON: Goethe again, the song of the South
stops.campa: On 17 November 1866 the Salle Favart gives Ambroise Thomas's Mignon, Barbier and Carré after Goethe's Wilhelm Meister — Goethe made song a second time. Célestine Galli-Marié is the waifish Mignon, the stolen Italian child who does not know her own country, and she sings the ache of it: 'Connais-tu le pays où fleurit l'oranger' — do you know the land where the orange flowers, the land of golden fruit and an eternal spring. It is Goethe's 'Kennst du das Land,' the very longing for the lemon-blossoming South that would one day drive Goethe himself across the Alps.
stops.quote: Connais-tu le pays où fleurit l'oranger, le pays des fruits d'or et des roses vermeilles... C'est là, c'est là que je voudrais vivre, aimer, aimer et mourir !
stops.quote_source: Mignon (Thomas), Act I — libretto Barbier & Carré, after Goethe

stops.name: Italy of the lemon-flower — Mignon's country, faced toward Goethe's Italian Journey
stops.campa: The country Mignon cannot name is Italy, and this stop faces Goethe's own Italian Journey. The land where the orange flowers, where the marble men beckon in the golden hall, where light boats glide like birds on a transparent lake — Goethe put that longing in his novel, and then obeyed it, slipping over the Brenner in 1786 toward Verona, Venice, Rome. Barbier's French carries the same yearning across another frontier and another art. Two journeys meet here: Goethe's real one south to the sun, and Mignon's sung one, homeward to a country she was stolen from and can only remember in song.
stops.quote: Kennst du das Land, wo die Zitronen blühn, im dunkeln Laub die Gold-Orangen glühn?
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre III — the German source Barbier translated
suggested_refs: Tischbein, Goethe in the Roman Campagna
View of Venice, the Grand Canal
sources: Cross-reference: goethe.journey.json (Italian Journey) in the atlas

segments.name: Shakespeare on the Seine — the tragedies set (1867-1868)

stops.name: Théâtre-Lyrique (Place du Châtelet) — ROMÉO ET JULIETTE
stops.campa: On 27 April 1867, in the new Théâtre-Lyrique on the Place du Châtelet, Gounod's Roméo et Juliette opens to the words of Barbier and Carré, as the Universal Exposition fills Paris with the world. Miolan-Carvalho is Juliette; the opera is a garland of duets, the lovers meeting and parting and meeting in song — 'Nuit d'hyménée, ô douce nuit d'amour!' Shakespeare's Verona is remade for the French pit, the balcony and the tomb strung between four love-duets. It is among Gounod's greatest triumphs, and the pair's Shakespeare turned wholly to music.
stops.quote: Nuit d'hyménée ! Ô douce nuit d'amour ! La destinée m'enchaîne à toi sans retour.
stops.quote_source: Roméo et Juliette (Gounod), Act IV duet — libretto Barbier & Carré, after Shakespeare
suggested_refs: Poster for Roméo et Juliette, Théâtre-Lyrique 1867
The Théâtre-Lyrique on the Place du Châtelet (now Théâtre de la Ville)

stops.name: Opéra (Salle Le Peletier) — HAMLET: the ghost and Ophelia's drowning
stops.campa: On 9 March 1868 the Salle Le Peletier gives Ambroise Thomas's Hamlet, Barbier and Carré after Shakespeare — the last great creation on that stage before it burned and the Garnier rose. Jean-Baptiste Faure is the brooding prince; Christine Nilsson is Ophélie, whose mad scene is the opera's glory: she wanders to the water's edge, sings her broken song to the willows, and drowns among the flowers. The ghost on the ramparts, the play within the play, the poisoned court — Shakespeare's darkest tragedy given a French tongue and, at the last, a French crown.
stops.quote: Partagez-vous mes fleurs !... À vous cette humble branche de romarin sauvage.
stops.quote_source: Hamlet (Thomas), Act IV, Ophélie's mad scene — libretto Barbier & Carré

stops.name: Elsinore of the mad Ophelia — the drowning faced as myth
stops.campa: The myth the opera enters stands on the cold battlements of Elsinore, where the murdered king walks and the prince feigns madness to unmask him. But the image that Barbier's verse fixes forever is Ophelia at the brook: her wits undone by grief and betrayal, she garlands herself with crow-flowers and long purples, climbs the leaning willow, and slips singing into the weedy water — 'her clothes spread wide, and mermaid-like awhile they bore her up.' Shakespeare's report becomes, in the opera, a scene we witness: madness set to a French coloratura, death by water made visible song.
stops.quote: There is a willow grows aslant a brook... There on the pendent boughs her coronet weeds clambering to hang, an envious sliver broke.
stops.quote_source: Shakespeare, Hamlet IV.vii — the source Barbier dramatized as Ophélie's mad scene

segments.name: The Besieged City — war, Commune, and Joan's consolation (1870-1873)

stops.name: Paris besieged — the theatres dark, the Franco-Prussian War
stops.campa: On 19 September 1870 the Prussian armies close the ring around Paris, and the lyric city falls silent. Sedan has fallen, the Empire is gone, the Republic proclaimed; through the long winter the capital starves, the theatres go dark, and the librettist's trade stops with them. There are no premieres now, only cold and cannon. The world that Carré and Barbier had filled with Faust and Juliette and Ophélie is a besieged city eating its zoo animals. It is an interruption in the poet's whole life — the one stretch of years when the myths cannot be made song.
suggested_refs: Photograph of the Siege of Paris, 1870-71

stops.name: The Commune and the burning — the Théâtre-Lyrique in flames
stops.campa: In the last days of May 1871 the Commune goes down in fire. As the government troops fight into the city, the Théâtre-Lyrique on the Place du Châtelet — where only four years before Roméo had sung to Juliette — burns to its walls on 25 May. The Tuileries, the Hôtel de Ville, whole quarters go up; Paris versifies its own tragedy in smoke. The stage that had carried Barbier's Shakespeare into song is a ruin. From this ash, the Third Republic will rise — and will look for something to console it. The librettist has an answer waiting: a maid of Lorraine.

stops.name: Argenteuil — the death of Michel Carré, the two-headed pen halved
stops.campa: On 28 June 1872, at Argenteuil on the Seine below Paris, Michel Carré dies. For more than twenty years the two names had been one signature — Carré et Barbier — so fused that no one could part their lines; now the pen is halved. Barbier will write on alone for thirty years more, and give some of his greatest work solo: the Contes d'Hoffmann, the Jeanne d'Arc. But the great collaborative engine of the Second Empire lyric stage is stopped. The survivor carries both names forward the way a widower carries a wedding ring — the myths still made song, but by one hand now.

stops.name: Théâtre de la Gaîté — JEANNE D'ARC: Joan as France's consolation
stops.campa: On 8 November 1873, at the Théâtre de la Gaîté by the square des Arts-et-Métiers, Barbier's own five-act verse drama Jeanne d'Arc is given with music by Gounod — this is Barbier not adapting but writing, his own alexandrines for the Maid. After the humiliation of 1870 and the amputation of Alsace-Lorraine, Joan of Lorraine returns to the Paris stage as the nation's wounded conscience: the peasant girl who heard the voices, drove out the invader, and burned for France. This stop faces our Joan of Arc journey directly — the martyr of Rouen made, in a beaten Paris, a promise of resurrection.
stops.quote: Filles de Lorraine, la Vierge est là qui vous appelle... pour la France, priez !
stops.quote_source: Jeanne d'Arc (Gounod), drame en cinq actes et en vers de Jules Barbier, 1873
suggested_refs: Engraving of Jeanne d'Arc at the Théâtre de la Gaîté, Le Monde Illustré 1873
Frémiet, equestrian Jeanne d'Arc, Place des Pyramides

stops.name: Domrémy and Rouen — the Maid's myth faced across the atlas
stops.campa: The myth the drama enters begins in a village of Lorraine and ends in the market-square of Rouen. This stop faces our Joan of Arc journey: the girl of Domrémy who at thirteen hears Saint Michael and Saint Catherine in her father's garden, cuts her hair, takes the sword, lifts the siege of Orléans, and crowns her king at Reims — then is sold, tried, and burned at nineteen, her ashes cast into the Seine. Barbier gives France, humbled in 1870, her holiest patriot back: not as history but as consolation, the martyr who proves the nation can rise from its own fire.
stops.quote: Voices? — I heard them well. They came from God.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, trial of condemnation, 1431 — the source-figure Barbier dramatized
suggested_refs: House of Joan of Arc, Domrémy
Site of the stake, Place du Vieux-Marché, Rouen
sources: Cross-reference: joan_of_arc.journey.json and falconetti.journey.json in the atlas

segments.name: The Last Enchantments — the solitary pen (1878-1882)

stops.name: Opéra (Palais Garnier) — POLYEUCTE: the Christian martyr
stops.campa: On 7 October 1878, in the year-old Palais Garnier, Gounod's Polyeucte is given to Barbier and Carré's verse after Corneille — the work Gounod loved above all his own, dreamed of years before in a church on the Via Appia. Polyeucte, newly baptized, smashes the pagan idols and will not recant though his wife Pauline pleads and the tribunal threatens; he goes to his death singing his faith. Corneille's great Christian tragedy is remade for the Opéra. But the age has cooled; the martyr fails to move the pit, and the work closes after twenty-nine nights — 'the sorrow of my life,' Gounod said.
stops.quote: Source délicieuse, en misères féconde, que vous versez de maux sur ceux qui vous font Dieu !
stops.quote_source: Polyeucte (Gounod), after Corneille — the stances Barbier adapted for the martyr
suggested_refs: Engraving of Polyeucte, Opéra 1878 (dessin de Vierge)

stops.name: Officier de la Légion d'honneur — the honors of the Third Republic
stops.campa: On 13 July 1880, on the eve of the first national Fête, the Republic promotes Barbier officier of the Légion d'honneur — he had been made chevalier back under the Empire, in August 1865. The dean of French librettists is honored not for one work but for a whole nation's evenings at the opera: it was through his verse that Goethe and Shakespeare, Corneille and Dante, Sheba and Joan reached the French ear as song. A man who never went to war or to sea has, by the labor of rhyme, carried the myths of Europe onto the stage of his one city.
suggested_refs: Cross of the Légion d'honneur, officier grade
Nadar portrait of Jules Barbier in later life

stops.name: Opéra-Comique (Salle Favart) — LES CONTES D'HOFFMANN: the poet and his automata
stops.campa: On 10 February 1881 the Salle Favart gives Les Contes d'Hoffmann — Barbier's late masterpiece, drawn from the play he and Carré wrote back in 1851, set by Offenbach, who died four months before the curtain rose. The poet Hoffmann tells his three loves: Olympia the wind-up doll, who sings 'Les oiseaux dans la charmille' until her spring runs down; Antonia, sung to her death; Giulietta, the courtesan who steals his mirror-image in Venice, where the Barcarolle floats over the lagoon — 'Belle nuit, ô nuit d'amour.' The mechanical woman, the muse, the notated song: the automaton made to sing.
stops.quote: Belle nuit, ô nuit d'amour, souris à nos ivresses ! Nuit plus douce que le jour, ô belle nuit d'amour !
stops.quote_source: Les Contes d'Hoffmann (Offenbach), the Barcarolle — text by Jules Barbier
suggested_refs: Poster for Les Contes d'Hoffmann, Opéra-Comique 1881
Olympia the singing automaton, costume/scene design

stops.name: Olympia's charmille — the automaton faced toward notation and the corpus's machines
stops.campa: The myth the tale enters is E.T.A. Hoffmann's own Germany of clockwork and delusion — this stop faces the corpus's threads of automata and notation. Olympia is the perfect singing machine, a doll of springs and gears whose aria winds down mid-phrase until a hand rewinds her; the poet, blinded by magic spectacles, loves a mechanism and does not know it. Here the sung human and the notated machine become the same thing: a body reduced to a score, a voice that is only its winding. The barcarolle's notation, the doll's mechanism — song written down until the writing sings by itself.
stops.quote: Les oiseaux dans la charmille, dans les cieux l'astre du jour, tout parle à la jeune fille d'amour !
stops.quote_source: Les Contes d'Hoffmann (Offenbach), Olympia's air — text by Jules Barbier
suggested_refs: E.T.A. Hoffmann, Der Sandmann, illustrated edition
sources: Cross-reference: laban.journey.json (Labanotation) and the corpus automata thread

stops.name: Opéra (Palais Garnier) — FRANÇOISE DE RIMINI: Dante on the operatic stage
stops.campa: On 14 April 1882 the Palais Garnier gives Ambroise Thomas's Françoise de Rimini, Barbier and Carré after Dante — the last opera of Thomas, and Barbier's Dantean stop. In a prologue drawn straight from Inferno V, the pilgrim Dante and his guide Virgil descend to the second circle, where the whirlwind of the lustful never rests, and Francesca da Rimini tells her tale: how she and Paolo read together of Lancelot, and how 'that day we read no further.' One kiss, one murder, one eternal storm. The Dantean cosmos — the very cosmos our atlas inscribes on-chain — turned to a French grand opéra.
stops.quote: Nessun maggior dolore che ricordarsi del tempo felice nella miseria — Il n'est pas de plus grande douleur que de se souvenir du temps heureux dans la misère.
stops.quote_source: Françoise de Rimini (Thomas), the prologue after Dante, Inferno V — libretto Barbier & Carré
suggested_refs: Ary Scheffer, The Ghosts of Paolo and Francesca

stops.name: The second circle of the Inferno — Paolo and Francesca faced toward the on-chain cosmos
stops.campa: The myth the opera enters is Dante's own Hell — this stop faces our on-chain Dantean cosmos directly. In the second circle the carnal sinners are swept forever in a black wind; among them Francesca da Rimini and her Paolo, cut down by her husband over an adulterous kiss. She tells the pilgrim how a book was their undoing — the romance of Lancelot — and how, at the fatal page, 'that day we read no further in it.' Where Dante fixed the lovers in terza rima and the corpus fixes his cosmos in the chain, Barbier fixes them in French verse to be sung: the whirlwind made audible.
stops.quote: Galeotto fu 'l libro e chi lo scrisse : quel giorno più non vi leggemmo avante. — Galeotto fut le livre, et celui qui l'écrivit ; ce jour-là nous n'y lûmes pas plus avant.
stops.quote_source: Dante, Inferno V.137 — the source-canto Barbier set as the opera's prologue
suggested_refs: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Paolo and Francesca da Rimini
sources: Cross-reference: the atlas's on-chain Dantean cosmos

segments.name: The Honors of the Republic — the last years (1883-1901)

stops.name: The Société des auteurs and the trade of the pen
stops.campa: In these late years Barbier is a pillar of the Société des auteurs et compositeurs dramatiques — the guild that defends the dramatist's right to be paid for every performance, the invention that lets a man live by his words. He knows its worth better than most: Les Noces de Jeannette alone has played a thousand times and more, and every night a librettist's royalty is owed. In 1887, when fire gutted the Opéra-Comique, he even served some months as its acting director. The bard of the corpus is also a man of the ledger, guarding the poet's bread.
suggested_refs: Seal of the Société des auteurs et compositeurs dramatiques

stops.name: The son Pierre Barbier — the pen handed on
stops.campa: The trade passes to the blood. Pierre Barbier, born in 1854, follows his father into the librettist's craft, and in the old man's last years the two write together — the opera Daphnis et Chloé among them, given in 1899. There had been a daughter too, Jeanne, born the year before Les Noces de Jeannette. The two-headed pen of Carré et Barbier, long since dissolved by Carré's death, becomes for a moment a father-and-son pen: the myths still being made song, now in a second Barbier hand, in the same Parisian rooms.

stops.name: Paris — death, 16 January 1901
stops.campa: On 16 January 1901, in Paris, Jules Barbier dies at seventy-five, in the century's first weeks — the last of the great Second Empire librettists, outliving Carré, Gounod, Thomas, and Offenbach, all of whom he had clothed in words. He had scarcely left his city; his journeys were the ones he sent others on — Faust to his bargain, Mignon to her lemon-flowering South, Sheba to Solomon, Joan to her fire, Francesca to her whirlwind. The corpus's own bard is stilled; but every night, somewhere, Marguerite still laughs into her mirror, and the Barcarolle still floats over the lagoon.
stops.quote: C'est là, c'est là que je voudrais vivre, aimer, aimer et mourir !
stops.quote_source: Mignon (Thomas), Act I — Barbier's own line, the longing that shaped a life of verse
